0d5a304993c65dff: From Raja Ahmad Fauzan
I refer to your report "Govt implementing 3 immediate flood mitigation measures in Shah Alam".

Three flood walls, flap gates and an outlet structure cost RM749,000. Six mobile pumps have also been deployed at four high-risk locations. The larger fix, a RM40 million project at Sungai Rasah, will not be ready until 2029 at the earliest.
So Shah Alam, a city drawn on paper before a single road was built, faces at least three more monsoons of moving cars to higher ground and lifting sofas onto bricks.

Walls and pumps are a mop. They clean up the water but do not turn off the tap. The profession is called flood mitigation, not flood reaction, because mitigation is what you do before the water arrives.

I learnt that in England. I was a design engineer on drainage and flood mitigation schemes for West Sussex county during my engineering career. Before anyone picked up a shovel, we ran storms through a computer model of the drainage network and watched where the water came out. Then we fixed it on screen, where mistakes are cheap.

A good model tells you things nobody wants to hear, such as the new estate upstream flooding the old one downstream. It is better to hear that from a computer than from a resident standing knee-deep in his living room.
Today, I run a business in Shah Alam, and I watch the water come out in real life.
Less rain, more planning

Some will say England and the Netherlands are not tropical, so the comparison is unfair. They are right about the rain. Kuala Lumpur receives roughly four times as much rain a year as London, and our storms are far more intense.
But the countries with gentler rain are the ones that plan hardest for it.

In England, anyone can type in an address and see the official flood map for free. Developers building in a flood-risk area must submit a flood risk assessment, which goes into the public planning file. Since November 2003, the Dutch have required water assessments for formal spatial plans, including consultation with water authorities. They built all of that for drizzle.
If a country with a quarter of our rain takes flooding this seriously, a tropical country should be doing more, not less.
A map nobody can look up

A flood hazard map for Selangor was presented to the state government in August 2025. The public can see flood hotspots on the state's Info Banjir site, but I cannot find the full map anywhere a homebuyer can look up an address.

In 2021, the irrigation and drainage department (JPS) commissioned a flood mitigation master plan study for the whole Klang River basin, at a cost of about RM2 million. It was due in late 2023 and was meant to produce flood risk maps.
Three years on, where is it? If it is finished, publish it. If it is not, tell us why.

That study matters because of how approvals work. Selangor developers must already hold back rainwater on their own sites and submit hydraulic studies. Last year, the federal government also said flood risk was a key factor in approving new housing.
But each project is studied on its own. Ten projects can each pass, and together still overload the same river. Only a basin-wide picture catches that.
A rulebook from 2012

JPS's web page of hydrology procedures, the basic methods for estimating rain and flood flows, lists 27 documents. Twenty-four are dated between 1973 and 1983. Some have since been revised, including for climate change, but the page, last updated in 2017, does not say so.

The Urban Stormwater Management Manual for Malaysia (MSMA) had its second edition published in 2011 and launched in 2012. A third edition has been in JPS's plans since at least 2021, and the department says a review is under way. There is still no new edition and no date.
Money is not the obstacle. JPS has about RM3.2 billion in this year's federal budget, roughly RM9 million a day.

Meanwhile, the National Water Research Institute of Malaysia (Nahrim) published guidance on how climate change will increase design rainfall as far back as 2013. That is good science. Yet I can find no public Nahrim study of flooding in Shah Alam, and no statement from it during a month in which the city flooded repeatedly.

Research that stays in a repository protects nobody. Nahrim should be the loudest voice in the room whenever a large project is approved upstream. It received about RM21 million in the 2026 budget. If we want it heard, fund it to be heard.
700 ponds, no clear owner
A detention pond full of silt holds no water. A drain full of rubbish is not a drain; it is a dam.
Selangor has nearly 700 detention ponds whose ownership and maintenance responsibility still need to be made clear.
Every pond and main drain here deserves a named owner, a budget and a cleaning schedule.
Give the rain somewhere to go

Pour a bucket of water on concrete and it runs everywhere. Pour it on grass and it disappears. Engineers call this a nature-based solution: instead of fighting the rain with bigger drains, you let the ground do what it did before we built on it.

In Britain, many car parks and walkways use permeable interlocking paving, blocks set over gravel so rain drains through the gaps and soaks away slowly. England has required planning permission since 2008 to pave more than five sq m of a front garden with an impermeable surface, unless suitable drainage is provided.
Same car park, same cost range, but one sends every drop to the drain, and the other holds it back.

Bigger versions exist too. Rotterdam has a public square that is a basketball court on dry days and fills like a bathtub in a storm, holding about 1.7 million litres. Mansfield built more than 300 rain gardens into its streets.
Shah Alam has fields, car parks, school compounds and road shoulders that could do the same.
Three things, in the open
To be fair, the state has a multi-billion ringgit flood programme, with Shah Alam next in line after Klang. The money is there. What is missing is the openness.
To JPS, publish the Selangor flood hazard map and the Klang basin study, and give us a date for the new MSMA.
To Nahrim, tell us plainly, in public, what the science says about Shah Alam's future rain.
To the state and MBSA, name the owner of every pond and main drain, and publish the cleaning schedule before the monsoon, not after.

Shah Alam was planned once. Plan it again, this time with the rain in mind. Otherwise, a few years from now we will be reading about the next three immediate measures. That would be flood reaction. We were promised mitigation.
Raja Ahmad Fauzan is the founder and CEO of Coffee Star, based in Shah Alam. He previously worked as a drainage and flood mitigation design engineer in West Sussex, England.

07aa889a1ecef497: LOS ANGELES: Inflation-weary US shoppers thronged malls and websites on Black Friday, the traditional kickoff to the holiday spending season, but many said they were struggling to find robust enough bargains to counter the pinch of high gas and grocery prices.
Spending is seen topping last year's strong figures by 4%-6%, forecasts show, but beneath top-line forecasts lie signs of stress.
Most of the gains will be attributable to inflation - which at 3.8% is about a percentage point higher than in each of the last two years - and consumer sentiment remains shaky.

Jasmine Peters, 37, went to the Westfield Century City mall in Los Angeles on Friday hoping to find steeper discounts in-store than online, but they didn't materialize, and by late morning, she was planning to leave the mall empty-handed.

Chris Nile, 30, was hoping for more than the US$50 discount he saw on a Nintendo Switch 2 gaming console, which brought the price to US$450. "Inflation is higher - hell, even the (McDonald's) McChicken is up," said Nile as he shopped for his two boys at the Crabtree Valley Mall in Raleigh, North Carolina.

Observers said consumers seemed less impressed by discounts, with stores needing to do more to draw them in. Target Corp, for example, gave away US$100 gift cards to the first 100 people in line at each store -- with one lucky recipient receiving a US$1,000 card.

"Traffic levels in general seemed off compared to past holidays and seemed to lose steam early," said Michael Brown, Americas retail leader at consulting firm Kearney, who visited several stores in Westchester County, New York, on Friday morning.

US store visits were tracking 2% behind last year's as of late afternoon, at 530 million a little after 3:30 pm US eastern time, according to Passby, a geospatial analytics company that measures real-time foot traffic.

A November survey by the National Retail Federation found that 82% of consumers are taking steps to manage holiday costs this year, like buying less expensive gifts. Nile - like many US shoppers - said he chose to bargain-hunt in person, in part to avoid shipping costs.

AI could also scramble the year's shopping dynamics. As consumers use it to find bargains or even complete purchases — and retailers become increasingly adept at altering prices — the deepest discounts could come closer to Christmas.

Online spending on Black Friday itself, though, was expected to jump 9.2% from a year ago to US$12.9 billion, according to a forecast from Adobe Analytics, the arm of Adobe that analyzes customer behavior.
Measured growth
Economic worries aside, top-line spending is expected to be robust.

Thanksgiving Day saw consumers spend US$7.1 billion online, according to Adobe, a 10.4% jump over last year, fueled by big discounts on electronics, toys and apparel. Indeed, store visits to electronics retailer Best Buy were tracking 4.4% higher than last Black Friday at midday, according to Passby. Visits to Walmart and Target were flat to slightly up.
Overall, the National Retail Federation sees November-December holiday retail sales rising 4.2% year-over-year, to just above $1 trillion.

High living costs emerged as a key issue earlier this month when voters handed Democrats sweeping electoral victories, punishing US President Donald Trump for an Iran war that's pushed the cost of living higher.
Even higher earners may be stretched.

Holiday spending forecasts mostly predated the recent stock market correction that followed the midterms, turmoil at chipmaker Nvidia, and mounting concerns around an AI bubble. The decline could dampen the wealth effect that has seen affluent shoppers splurge, UBS analysts said in a note on Tuesday.
Embattled toys
Higher input costs, particularly from oil derivatives like plastic, are hitting some products more than others.
Prices of toys — generally high in plastic — have risen 13.2% since the start of the year, pushing Barbie maker Mattel this month to cut its annual forecast as consumers balked at higher costs.

But some unlikely products are buoying the toy category. Best Buy and Target have both flagged trading cards — including Pokemon and Magic: The Gathering products — as a key growth driver. Squishy NeeDoh toys are also in hot demand, according to e-commerce marketing platform Omnisend.

Lego also appeared to be in high demand, with the Passby figures showing its stores' foot traffic up more than 5% in mid-afternoon versus the same time of day last Black Friday. It wasn't necessarily kids driving the growth - most of those online were adults, part of the "kidult" craze that has swept the toy industry in recent years.
Jaime Oquendo, 46, was the first to enter the Lego store at the Westfield Century City mall in Los Angeles when it opened, to buy a new Godzilla set, released on Black Friday at US$450.
“I actually made sure I had money set aside all year, back when they announced it, just to make sure I could get my hands on one,” Oquendo said.

9c04dfa0fc0222e8: From Moaz Nair
Whenever political temperatures rise, the same old script is replayed: DAP is a threat to the position of the Malays and the sanctity of Islam.

However, if we set aside emotional sentiment and evaluate the situation based on demographic realities, the Federal Constitution, and the latest 2027 budget, this narrative is clearly more of a political gimmick than fact.
Logically speaking, how could a party often labelled a "Chinese party" possibly seize absolute power in this country?

The Chinese community makes up only about 20% of the total citizenry in Malaysia, and not all of them vote for DAP. With numbers this small, it is impossible for any Chinese-dominated party to form a government on its own, let alone alter the fundamental structure of the nation.

More importantly, the pillars of national power remain firmly in Malay hands. From the institution of the Malay rulers and the office of the prime minister, right down to the top leadership of the civil service, the armed forces and police, all are led by Malays.
Fears that Malay political power will be eroded are simply manufactured anxieties.
Respecting the constitution and social contract
The track record since the formation of the unity government proves that DAP respects the Federal Constitution.

As acknowledged by Umno leaders themselves, DAP leaders have never questioned Article 153 regarding the special position of the Malays and Bumiputeras, the status of Islam as the religion of the federation, or Bahasa Melayu as the national language.
In fact, when the government organised the Bumiputera Economic Congress to strengthen the Malay economic agenda, DAP voiced no objections.
This proves the party supports efforts to empower Islam and the Bumiputera economy, so long as they operate within the constitutional framework without denying the rights of other races.
Latest proof in the 2027 budget
Anti-Islam accusations also flatly contradict the government allocations approved alongside DAP cabinet ministers.
In the 2027 federal budget, allocations for Islamic affairs are not only untouched, they surge to RM3.1 billion compared to RM2.6 billion previously.

This substantial funding covers full Socso contributions for 40,000 mosque officials and takmir teachers, special incentives for Kafa teachers, as well as the establishment of the Malaysian Pondok and Turath Advisory Council.
In Penang, which has been led by DAP since 2008, the Malay community and Islamic institutions continue to be empowered.

Through the 2027 state budget, chief minister Chow Kon Yeow’s administration is fully funding the construction of three new mosques worth RM14 million (in addition to a RM3.9 million contribution for Masjid Cherok Tok Kun Atas), allocating RM15.07 million to build three Sekolah Agama Rakyat, and channelling one-off special aid to Kafa, tahfiz, and pondok teachers.
Furthermore, DAP-elected representatives nationwide continue to actively serve the Malay communities in their respective constituencies regardless of background.
Exemplary DAP ministerial performance

Rather than pursuing any racial agenda, DAP ministers have built a strong reputation for administrative competence and tangible delivery that directly benefits all Malaysians - the majority of whom are Malay and Bumiputera.
At the transport ministry, Loke Siew Fook earned widespread praise for a no-nonsense, data-driven approach to fixing public infrastructure.

He enforced strict reliability targets that significantly reduced LRT breakdowns, digitalised road tax and licence renewals via the MyJPJ app to eliminate long queues, cracked down on overloaded lorries to make highways safer, and kept major projects like the East Coast Rail Link and Johor Bahru–Singapore RTS Link firmly on track.

Meanwhile, since taking over the Federal Territories portfolio in December 2025, Hannah Yeoh - the first Kuala Lumpur MP to hold the post in two decades - has delivered immediate, practical relief to urban residents.

She halved DBKL rental rates for over 10,000 petty traders, lowered Ramadan bazaar site fees to RM400, channelled RM300 million into upgrading all 51 public housing areas, gazetted over 550 permanent green spaces, and rolled out 13 governance reforms to break tender cartels and tighten anti-corruption oversight.

Similarly, under housing and local government minister Nga Kor Ming, Malaysia surpassed its target of building 500,000 affordable homes, revived over 1,500 abandoned housing projects to rescue around 176,000 homebuyers, and completed more than 15,000 public infrastructure upgrades nationwide.
Across the board, DAP ministers have focused squarely on modernising public services and uplifting communities across all races.
Not a single race party

It is often forgotten that DAP is not an exclusive club for one race. The party’s membership and leadership include many Malaysians of Malay, Indian, and Orang Asli descent, as well as the indigenous peoples of Sabah and Sarawak.
Today, DAP leaders and ministers are focused on their core duties - driving the economy and solving the people’s problems - which ultimately uplifts all races.
Critics often claim the current government is subservient to DAP because the party holds a large number of parliamentary seats within Pakatan Harapan.
However, if there is truly any hidden agenda to undermine Islam or the Malays, prove it through legal channels and the courts, rather than relying on rhetoric on the ceramah stage.

Malaysians deserve a more mature brand of politics. It is high time we judge any political party based on its work performance and tangible contributions to the nation, rather than falling into the trap of the politics of fear deliberately stoked for the narrow interests of a few.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

a3c2df64e8bf674e: Human rights groups reiterated that to get true justice in Myanmar, the junta rule must end
Originally published on Global Voices
Rohingya refugee camp in Bangladesh. Photo by CAPTAIN RAJU. Source: Wikipedia. CC BY-SA 4.0

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled on November 19 that Myanmar’s military forces committed genocide against the Rohingya people during a brutal 2017 crackdown in the western Rakhine state.

Voting 9–6, the ICJ verdict found the military’s “clearance operations,” which led to the mass murder of at least 10,000 people and the forced expulsion of more than 700,000 Rohingya to the neighboring country of Bangladesh, constituted genocidal acts.

Myanmar has more than one hundred ethnic groups but refuses to recognize the Rohingya, who are considered illegal immigrants even though they were born in Myanmar, and many have been there for generations. The Rohingya have been viciously persecuted for decades and targeted by hate speech and violent acts not just by state forces but also by hardline Buddhist nationalists.
It was The Gambia, with the support of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, that initiated the ICJ complaint in November 2019.

This is the first time the ICJ has found a state liable for committing genocide. The Myanmar military government, which grabbed power in a February 2021 coup, described the decision as unfair and a “great disappointment” while pointing out that the verdict was not unanimous.
The National Unity Government of Myanmar, which represents the pro-democracy forces, said in a statement that the pursuit of justice cannot be realized without ending the junta rule.

“The ICJ judgment is an important step in the pursuit of justice, but it cannot be the end. Lasting peace requires accountability, protection for all communities and the dismantling of the structures that enable persecution and impunity.”

The ICJ ruling was eagerly awaited, especially by Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh. In one interview, 58-year-old Monajat Alam from one of the refugee camps shared, “The Myanmar military tried to convince the world that we had lied. Today, the truth has been recognized.”
Here’s the reaction in a Rohingya refugee camp in Bangladesh to the International Court of Justice ruling that Myanmar committed the crime of genocide https://t.co/OUxhAg5qBn
— Elaine Pearson (@PearsonElaine) November 19, 2026
Shwe Maung, a former Member of Parliament in Myanmar, emphasized that unity and national reconciliation cannot be achieved without recognizing the need to attain justice for the Rohingya.

As a former Member of Myanmar’s Parliament representing Buthidaung Township, I have long maintained that justice for the Rohingya and justice for the wider population of Myanmar are not competing causes.
They are inseparable.
Myanmar cannot build genuine federal democracy, national reconciliation, or lasting peace while denying grave crimes committed against one of its communities.
The Karen National Union, which represents the Karen ethnic community, reiterated the call to hold the Myanmar military accountable.

“The same Myanmar military that committed genocide against the Rohingya continues to commit atrocities against civilian communities across Burma. We must keep working together to bring justice to all the people of Burma who have suffered these crimes.”

The UN Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Myanmar, Kelley E. Currie, hailed the ICJ ruling. “Today the world court has called the crimes by their true name: genocide. That name matters. It is a recognition of what was done, and it puts us on the path to justice.”

The Special Advisory Council for Myanmar highlighted the call to sustain the verdict with decisive action. “Justice has been decided, but not yet delivered,” said Yanghee Lee, a founding member of the council.
Rohingya refugees, Burmese people react to ICJ Myanmar genocide ruling

Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh express “immense happiness and emotion” after the International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the minority group. https://t.co/rEQowEqYDZ
— AFP News Agency (@AFP) November 23, 2026
Human rights activist Razia Sultana, who testified about the horrific violence endured by Rohingya women, asserted the urgency of ending the atrocities committed by the junta.
For the women who shared their testimonies with me, justice cannot remain only a judgment written on paper.
It must mean safety, recognition, accountability and the opportunity to rebuild their lives.
I think again of the women I met in the refugee camps, of what they described and the courage it took to speak.
Their voices travelled from the camps to the United Nations Security Council and became part of the wider international struggle for justice.
Thinzar Shunlei Yi shared the impact of the ruling on pro-democracy activists like her.
This verdict brings a sense of healing for me, too. It feels as though one of the chronic diseases Myanmar suffer has finally been named.
Having faced oppression myself as a woman and a political dissident, I know the scale of their suffering is incomparable—yet so many of us desperately needed to see that justice is possible.
Journalist Nyein Chan Aye is concerned over the recent rise of social media posts inciting hate against the Rohingya.

Rohingya civilians are not the enemies of Rakhine Buddhists, nor are Rakhine civilians the enemies of the Rohingya. Neither community is the enemy of Myanmar’s people. Their grievances and rights cannot be settled by another campaign of suspicion and hatred.

Around 14 countries have already acknowledged the ICJ ruling. Sanctions have been imposed as well by the United Kingdom government on senior military officers of Myanmar. Meanwhile, China raised the issue of “jurisdiction overreach and expanded interpretation” and warned that the ruling could undermine the settlement of disputes.

The junta remains in power, but pro-democracy forces are relentless in the struggle to restore civilian rule. Millions of stateless Rohingya are scattered in various camps, but the landmark ICJ ruling is a step forward in the pursuit of justice and the advancement of the demand to allow the persecuted minority to return to their home.
Written by Mong Palatino

Don't expect things to get better in the short term, as Counterpoint forecasts another 6 percent drop during 2027. But it believes that the market may see a 6 percent rebound in 2028, as memory supplies improve, pricing begins to stabilize, and pent-up demand for replacement phones returns.

The 2026 outlook has been shaped by sharply rising component costs, particularly for DRAM and NAND flash. According to IDC, memory costs have risen approximately 350 percent since last year and are still climbing.

As Reg readers will be well aware by now, this has been blamed on the memory manufacturers prioritizing output of high-margin chips to go into AI servers and GPU accelerators, creating a shortage of the mainstream components that are needed for devices like PCs and phones.

Vendors have responded by raising prices, reducing memory configurations, and withdrawing lower-cost models. As The Register previously reported, memory costs accounted for almost 60 percent of the total bill of materials in sub-$400 smartphones during Q1 of 2026.

For 2027, Counterpoint warns the outlook is for continued tight mobile DRAM supply, further price increases for low-power DDR (LPDDR) memory, and limited evidence to suggest short-term capacity increases.
"The 2026 decline was initially expected to mark the low point of the cycle, but the memory situation has remained more restrictive than anticipated," said principal analyst Yang Wang.

"Mobile memory allocation is still being displaced by AI and server demand, while higher costs are taking longer to move through handset portfolios and retail channels. The result is a much weaker 2027, particularly for lower priced devices and price sensitive markets."
Global shipments are forecast to rebound by 6 percent in 2028, but that would bring shipments only roughly back to this year's already shrunken level, rather than hitting the peak of previous years.
Counterpoint cautions that the scale of the rebound will depend on how quickly lower component costs translate into retail pricing.

A speedy improvement in mobile memory allocation during the second half of 2027 could bring replacement demand forward and swell shipments, but continued competition from the AI market or another round of handset price increases would hinder recovery.

"The unusually low 2027 base creates the potential for a robust rebound in 2028 once the memory bottleneck begins to ease. But this should not be interpreted as a return to the old market trajectory," Wang said.
"Some low-end demand has been permanently lost, and the 2028 market will still be about 14 percent below 2025 shipments."
Potential availability of 6G-capable smartphones toward the end of the decade could give the market a boost, but Counterpoint does not expect it to regain its 2025 shipment levels by 2030. ®

d1172e44d2bf9820: Birmingham City Council faces a £128.1 million bill for its disastrous transition from SAP to Oracle – more than six times the original estimate for a project that contributed to its financial collapse.

Papers presented to its Audit Committee this week put the combined cost of the original implementation, which went live in 2022, and this year's reimplementation at £128.1 million, against £19.96 million forecast in the 2019 business case [PDF].
The report, from program director Philip Macpherson, said the project's funding allocation had previously reached £157 million.
The report said the new Oracle Fusion system went live in August without any priority-one or "showstopper" issues.
"The program has now moved into the Post Go Live Support phase where [it] continues to provide extra support but slowly transitions towards 'Business As Usual' operating procedures," the report said.
It is an understatement to say the same was not true of the first attempt to move the council's finance, HR, and payroll systems off its legacy R/3 SAP system to more modern software.

The first project started in 2019 and was supposed to go live in April 2021, but was delayed by a year. After the council started to use the system in April 2022, it soon became beset by a series of serious problems.

Although the council had planned to implement Oracle "out-of-the-box," it created several customizations, including a bank reconciliation system that failed to function properly. The council struggled to understand its cash position and was unable to produce auditable accounts. It has spent more than £5 million on manual workaround labor. The system move also contributed to it becoming effectively bankrupt, an event it failed to foresee due to the malfunctioning finance system.

It later emerged that officials ignored a "red" warning prior to the go-live date. They were explicitly told the system could cause late payments, a failure to collect debt, and incorrect accounting if it went live. Officials gave the go-ahead regardless.
The council decided to reimplement Oracle from scratch, while running the current system as best it could and implementing off-the-shelf software CivicaPay, now rebranded as Civica Income Management.
Despite the apparently trouble-free relaunch, the true cost to the council is likely higher than the projected £128.1 million implementation bill.
For a start, the original £19 million budget was supposed to support the software implementation for schools, but that was excluded from the reimplementation.
Secondly, the council expected significant savings from moving to Oracle in 2022 through greater efficiency. The 2019 business case booked £27 million in savings from 2019 to 2031, for example.

A 2024 analysis by Audit Reform Lab, based at the University of Sheffield, estimated that the disaster's direct and indirect financial impact, including lost savings and deteriorating tax collection, would reach £216.5 million by April 2026.
Council taxpayers can be assured the new system has gone live without major problems, but that is hardly cause for celebration. ®

ab9a7b7cc5d1247c: The UK government has rejected calls for a UK-wide public consultation on the environmental impacts of AI datacenters, despite a petition attracting more than 39,000 signatures.

Campaign group Protect the Wild launched the petition last month, calling for a national consultation that would consider whether further expansion should be restricted, paused, or halted until those impacts are properly understood and addressed.

The nonprofit says the petition smashed the 10,000 signature threshold above which a government response is required in just three days, and the total stood at over 39,000 as this article was being prepared.

In its response, published on November 23, the government ruled out the requested UK-wide environmental consultation, saying individual projects' impacts should be addressed through the planning process. It pointed instead to a separate consultation on its draft datacenter planning policy, open until January 8, 2027.

"Datacenters are vital to the UK's digital economy. They underpin the digital services that people rely on every day, including public services, healthcare and the way people work. They also provide the infrastructure needed to develop and use AI," the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) says.

"Building more capacity in the UK will support economic growth and innovation, while strengthening national resilience and ensuring the UK is well placed to realize the opportunities presented by AI."

But it adds that the government recognizes the environmental impacts of bit barns are real and must be understood and mitigated, and this is one of the reasons why it established the Data Centre Covenant tests.

This Covenant, published last month, sets out tests all compute sheds "are encouraged to meet," while "strategic datacenters" are required to meet them to qualify for additional government assistance.

The government has yet to define which datacenters qualify as "strategic," saying it will publish further details and eligibility criteria in due course. Qualifying projects could receive help securing power and accelerating planning.

Briefly, the Covenant tests are that operators cover any energy costs they create, so that communities do not have to pick up the bill; that they invest in local communities; adhere to the highest environmental standards; create jobs and drive reindustrialization; and provide secure and reliable access to their compute resources.

If this has a ring of familiarity, it is because President Trump earlier this year introduced a Ratepayer Protection Pledge, under which hyperscalers and AI companies agreed to protect US consumers from any bill shocks due to the energy and infrastructure requirements of their datacenter projects. It seems that where the US leads, the UK still often follows.
The Covenant sets out efficiency targets and reporting expectations, but does not explain how compliance will be enforced or specify penalties for failing to meet its tests.
Protect the Wild notes that it "barely acknowledges wildlife, habitats or biodiversity. In fact, it doesn't mention any of those things at all."
The Covenant does, however, call on operators to "protect nature," without spelling out specific safeguards for wildlife, habitats, or biodiversity.

While the government encourages all server farms to meet the tests, only those it considers "strategic" are required to do so, as we noted above. And even that is only in order to qualify for extra government support, not in order to gain approval for a project.

Further, the campaign group contends that having environmental concerns addressed on a project-by-project basis at the planning level is a major barrier to tackling greenhouse gas emissions at a national level.

It cites the draft National Policy Statement for Data Centres, under which operational emissions from nationally significant projects in England, including those from on-site power generation, would be managed against national climate commitments at an economy-wide level rather than assessing each application's contribution to those targets.

Protect the Wild also argues that project-level assessments do not adequately capture nationwide habitat loss, even though the planning process requires consideration of cumulative environmental effects.

Datacenters have become a growing public concern in the UK, although opposition has not reached the level it has in the US, where anti-datacenter sentiment played a major part in political campaigns for the recent midterm elections.

But there were protests around the country at the start of November, such as in London and at Great Torrington, a town in Devon where a proposed 1.5 GW data campus and battery energy storage facility would cover 850 acres of nearby farmland.
Celebrity TV cook Delia Smith recently joined protests over a proposed datacenter on the edge of Norwich in Norfolk over concerns it may threaten a nearby nature reserve.

Protesters are unlikely to find much sympathy in Westminster. The government has already pinned its hopes for growing the economy on AI, as detailed in its AI Opportunities Action Plan last year, and it sees building more datacenters as key to achieving this.

The Guardian reports that Natural England, the government's own advisory body for the natural environment, is being threatened with abolition weeks after raising objections to a large AI campus near Bristol because of the threat it poses to protected wildlife and habitats.

A separate report found that the government met with 137 different businesses to discuss datacenters between July 2024 and June 2026, but did not meet a single community group or environmental organization during the same period. ®

668efd6679523792: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 27 — The World Bank’s downward revision of its 2026 global growth forecast does not signal an impending recession, according to World Bank economist Deisigan Shammugam.
He said the global economy was still expanding, but more slowly and with higher inflation.
About two-thirds of economies now face weaker growth prospects than the World Bank projected in January, largely due to the economic fallout from the Middle East crisis, he said.
“The revised outlook should not be interpreted as a recession warning.

“And just to be clear, it is not a recession call. The world keeps growing, but more slowly and with higher inflation,” Deisigan said yesterday at the National Economic Outlook Conference organised by the Malaysian Institute of Economic Research (MIER) here.
Why the slowdown in 2026?
Deisigan said one of the biggest shocks was the Middle East crisis, which was working its way through the economy via several channels.
“We’ve had many energy crises in the past and the four channels are very familiar: energy prices, inflation, interest rates and tighter financial conditions.
“We are pretty well aware of these channels, but what is really different this time is the shipping and the supply chain,” he said.
He said the World Bank report pointed to broader disruptions to global supply chains and higher input costs.
“It shows in retail fuel prices like diesel.
“Since March, wholesale prices of diesel and jet fuel have climbed considerably more than crude oil, while refining spreads are hovering well beyond their historical norms.
“So it is no surprise that AirAsia is finding it difficult this time around,” he said.

Deisigan cautioned policymakers against relying on Brent crude prices alone to estimate retail pump prices, as shipping disruptions, supply constraints and sharply higher insurance costs for tanker fleets were also pushing up costs.

“So if you proxy Brent to retail using just the APM formula like how we do in Malaysia, you are going to miss the market price, the true market price of the retail price,” he said, referring to the Automatic Pricing Mechanism.

He added that global oil supply is projected to fall by around 5 per cent this year due to production cuts linked to the Strait of Hormuz crisis, with gains elsewhere offsetting only a small share of the Middle East losses.
“Consumption is also expected to fall 2.5 per cent, the third-largest decline in energy consumption on record,” Deisigan said.
He said global growth was expected to pick up to 2.8 per cent in both 2027 and 2028 as energy supplies recover, monetary easing resumes and trade strengthens.

Among emerging market and developing economies, growth is projected to slow from 4.4 per cent to 3.6 per cent, while China’s growth is expected to ease to 4.2 per cent amid weakness in its property sector, labour market and consumer confidence.

However, the World Bank expects that if the recent increase in crude shipments from the Gulf proves durable, global oil production will recover towards 2025 levels in 2027, consumption will rebound slightly, and the market will return to surplus by the second quarter of next year.
Turning to financial markets, Deisigan said emerging economies could face greater uncertainty as fiscal vulnerabilities and high debt levels in major economies push up global borrowing costs.
He said rising fiscal risks could increase the term premium demanded by investors, potentially raising borrowing costs across markets.
Deisigan also warned that increasingly concerned investors could move their money out of emerging markets into safer assets, particularly from economies seen as having weak governance.
He said this made structural reforms and stronger governance important for emerging economies seeking to maintain investor confidence.
“The solution, sorry to say, boring old answer from an economist: structural policies are the answer,” he said.

Europe's fastest growing categories are datacenter systems, forecast to grow 29.7 percent in 2027, and infrastructure as a service, at 26.7 percent.
Even so, Lovelock does not expect Europe to compete with North America and China on AI investment.

"For AI provision, Europe is going to be behind, and there won't be a way to catch up," he said. "The AI datacenters, the large language models, the foundational models, the tools and techniques for building out AI are all being centered outside of Europe, but enterprises don't need to do that. So the question becomes: regardless of where the source of the AI is coming from, can the enterprises actually adopt and use it? In one sense, Europe will be behind in the provision of AI, but it need not be behind in the use."

The gap nonetheless complicates Europe's push to reduce its dependence on US technology suppliers. The European Union has introduced new rules to encourage tech buyers to favor sovereign tech over the dominant tech vendors, but Lovelock doubts they will move spending much.
"Sovereignty is a wonderful flag that we fly on the front of a building. IT is running in the basement. CIOs are not going to buy a second-best solution that costs more simply because it's sovereign.

"They are not going to break any laws, but they are not going to make a decision that puts their company in a worse position at a higher cost. While sovereignty gets [vendors] on the list, it doesn't assure that they get purchased," he told us.

Earlier this month, Gartner predicted that by 2029, more than 90 percent of EU organizations will have a digital sovereignty strategy, but argued that a fully sovereign technology stack remains out of reach.
"The global technology supply chain is too interconnected, and many critical dependencies cannot be replaced at a commercially viable scale," said Bettina Tratz-Ryan, VP analyst at Gartner. ®

0ae2924ce73a0941: The AI building boom is driving up optical networking equipment prices and stretching delivery times to as much as 18 months, according to network operator RETN.
RETN says that network operators and telcos are now directly competing with AI datacenters for chips and other components.

As Reg readers will be aware, memory prices have soared by four or five times over the past year or so, but RETN says optical networking equipment prices have risen by around 50 percent since the start of 2026. Worse are the extended delivery times, with optical network kit that used to arrive within three months now taking 12 to 15, and some orders taking up to 18 months.

This is as bad as, if not worse than, the shortages during the pandemic, when chip supply problems left network vendors unable to fulfill orders. The issue now is that because of the AI boom, demand is outpacing supplies.
In its report, "AI, Connected," RETN says developers building outside established datacenter hubs may need to involve network carriers two to five years before opening.

The sudden demand for network kit from hyperscalers and AI campuses is only one factor, RETN says. Raw material shortages, skilled labor shortages, energy constraints, geopolitical tensions, and logistical challenges are also compounding the issue.
However, it concedes that many carriers didn't help themselves by previously postponing network upgrades to cut expenditure. That work has now become unavoidable at the worst possible time.

Network diversity is now seen as a must-have, the report says. Where customers were once satisfied with two routes to long-haul destinations, they expect operators to provide four or more redundant routes now.

The aim is to prevent a single failure from taking down critical services. Multiple connections are only useful protection if they avoid shared physical failure points, such as the same ducts or cable routes. A diverse circuit might cost €1,800 ($1,975) a month instead of €600 ($658), it claims, but an outage could prove far more costly.

RETN also says AI datacenters are moving away from populated areas to remote locations, where access to suitable land, power and water may be easier to come by. Hyperscalers are building in the Nordics, where land is affordable, the climate is cooler, and plenty of renewable energy is available.
Remote sites may lack the fiber infrastructure needed to connect them to other datacenters and customers. The Register reported on this issue earlier this year.

For sites close to cities, developers often fund the fiber themselves, which adds just a few percent to the total project cost. But over longer distances, the case becomes harder to make, and carriers are understandably reluctant to build a long-haul route to serve a single remote site.

Some developers are prepared to swallow the cost: RETN says a major cloud provider is exploring converting an abandoned factory in Central Europe into a large-scale server farm, despite little existing fiber in the area.
However, RETN's warning is that connectivity must be planned alongside power and construction, not left until the datacenter is nearly ready to open. ®

63167c3504ee3f27: Over the last few weeks, I’ve been talking to Alexander (Avi) Davidson. There are a lot of remarkable things about Avi. He sustained a horrific injury as a teenager, which left him paralyzed and without a left hand. Today, he uses his own experience to guide his practice as a trauma therapist.

He’s also taking part in a clinical trial of some new tech that allows him to move—and feel with—a prosthetic hand. Unlike standard prosthetics, this one connects directly to nerves in Avi’s arm. He literally has wires coming out of his arm to plug it in with.
Avi’s the ninth person to trial this tech. But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently, for things like drinking from a cup (which is not easy) and writing (also not easy).
What struck me the most over our conversations was Avi’s outlook and approach to not just his injuries and learning to use this cutting-edge technology, but to life itself.

He has learned how to use something like seven different prosthetics in the 17 years since his accident. By taking part in this trial, he’s had to fit hundreds of hours of lab-based training and physical therapy around his demanding job. He had surgery to implant electrodes in his arm and will eventually need another to remove them. And he won’t even get to keep the latest prosthetic long term.

“While it’s unfortunate at times, and irritating at times, I do not regret what has come from [the accident], or the fact that it happened,” he told me. “I am not going to benefit from this … I wanted to be a part of this in the context of being able to help push the technology forward.”

The research team at the University of Utah that is running the trial hopes it will answer longstanding questions about the technology. How does it fare in a real-world setting, outside of the lab? What do people end up using it for? Where can improvements be made?

There may be some surprises along the way. Avi has found that his prosthetic wrist can feel sore and stiff when it’s been overused, just like his flesh-and-blood wrist. Weirdly, that feeling can be relieved by stretching it out. What’s going on here? No one really knows.

Scientists don’t know whether Avi’s brain will change as a result of using the bionic hand, either. Before the trial started, they performed brain scans to see how his missing left hand was represented in his brain. Will that change? And what might that mean for people who are born without limbs—how might a bionic limb affect their brains?

Avi will have the device until late January 2027 at the least, and potentially for another year. After that? Again, no one knows. It will depend on how the research is progressing, how Avi feels, and how much funding the team can secure. As a result, it’s not clear how long the device might even be expected to last in a person’s body.
I’ll be following this study, though, and will keep you posted.
This article first appeared in The Checkup, MIT Technology Review’s weekly biotech newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Thursday, and read articles like this first, sign up here.

fd03cdaa4510b90c: Britain's Royal Navy is investing £142 million ($185 million) in underwater drones to tackle sea mines, but the contract has gone to an American defense supplier.
The Ministry of Defence (MoD) says that the UK's ability to protect vital sea routes will be strengthened through the procurement of these Uncrewed Underwater Vehicles (UUVs).
These will form part of the Royal Navy's move toward a "Hybrid Navy" comprising a mix of crewed, uncrewed, and autonomous platforms in order to meet future challenges.

The UUV selected for the job is the REMUS 620, built by Huntington Ingalls Industries (HII), the largest military shipbuilding company in the United States. HII has a facility at Portchester, on the south coast of England, but is still a US-owned company.
We asked the MoD how the award fits its pledge to prioritize buying British wherever possible, and what share of the contract's value will support UK industry.

The contract includes HII's Sea Launcher automated launch and recovery systems and will bring support services previously delivered overseas to the UK. HII says it will support 15 jobs, while the MoD identifies Portchester among the locations benefiting.

HII says this is the largest international order in its 25-year history of supplying uncrewed systems. The MoD has previously acquired REMUS 100, REMUS 300, and REMUS 600 vehicles for mine countermeasure operations.
The new vehicles will locate sea mines to support clearance operations and help keep shipping routes open.

By using drones to comb a body of water for explosive devices, the Royal Navy's crews can be kept a safe distance from any potential immediate threat. Traditionally, this work has been conducted by specialist crewed ships such as the Hunt class or Sandown class, but these are being retired from service in favor of uncrewed systems.
The Royal Navy also operates SWEEP, an uncrewed boat towing equipment that mimics a ship's magnetic, acoustic, and electric signatures to trigger mines from a safe distance.
The new REMUS underwater vehicles can be sent ahead of other vessels to search beneath the surface, making minehunting operations safer, faster and more flexible, according to the MoD.
"This investment strengthens our ability to protect freedom of navigation, which is critical to our security and our economy," said Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP.

Like others in the portfolio, REMUS 620 resembles a naval torpedo. It is capable of operating at depths of 600 meters and has an endurance of up to 110 hours on a single mission. The drones will be integrated with SeeTrack and Neptune software developed by SeeByte in the UK, which is already used by the Royal Navy.

In trials announced in October 2025, a REMUS 620 demonstrated launch and recovery using a submerged test fixture replicating a Virginia-class submarine's torpedo tube. The work could enable submarines to deploy and retrieve underwater drones on future missions. ®

Ripple effect

But once it broke, swift action by authorities contained any systemic risk, against a backdrop of economic challenges including higher energy prices due to the Iran war, analysts said. "In the past at times of stress in the Turkish economy, Turkish households would start exchanging their savings into hard currency, maybe buy more gold as an insurance," said Magdalena Polan, head of emerging markets macroeconomic research at PGIM.

Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz said on Thursday that 199 billion lira (US$3.93 billion) had been paid back, and that authorities would take steps to protect investors.
'Made to beg for our own money'
Savers among the nearly half a million who invested in the funds are angry over what they see as corruption.

At a protest outside the SPK headquarters in Ankara last week attended by several hundred people, some savers demanded full repayment, with several describing how they unsuccessfully sought to sell their investments as the funds imploded.
"We have been made to beg for our own money," said Murat Galip Alparslan, a roofer, adding that he had lost 26 years of his own savings as well as money saved by his mother.
"My family's future has been stolen," he said.

Criminal complaints are being filed over trades in stocks that took place up to two years ago and should have been referred to prosecutors much sooner, said Basak, who expects "hundreds of trades" to come under scrutiny in court.

a03f78dab76c974e: ‘All we want is peace; there will be no peace without equal rights and justice.’
Originally published on Global Voices
Jhiko Manyika performing at Zanzibar Reggae Festival. Image by Zanzibar Reggae Festival, used with permission.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.
When courts stop protecting people, people stop talking. They stay quiet because speaking up could cost them their lives or their families. So who speaks for the voiceless?

In Tanzania, one answer comes with a guitar. Reggae artist Jhikoman, born Jhikolabwino Siza Manyika, has released a song called “Justice,” written for everyone who lost a loved one, and the right to mourn them out loud, after the October 2025 general elections that declared Samia Suluhu Hassan president.
His favorite lyric sums up the song:
“We don’t need no war, all we want is peace; there will be no peace without equal rights and justice.”
Listen to Justice below:
Tanzania’s image shattered

For nearly six decades, Tanzania cultivated an image of calm, consensus, and order. The scale of the 2025 election violence shocked many people because it broke that image. The BBC reported that security forces and unrest killed more than 500 people. International observers criticized the vote for its lack of transparency, and the African Union and the Southern African Development Community (SADC) said the election fell short of democratic standards.
Jhikoman, who watched these events unfold, says the losses moved him to write. He told Global Voices:

“I was deeply moved by reports and accounts of people losing their lives, families losing their loved ones, and citizens being silenced by the authorities when they simply wanted to speak out, seek answers, and mourn those they had lost. That pain became my motivation to write ‘Justice.’”
This song is more than a song; it is a cry for humanity, a call for accountability, and a reminder that the pain of those who have lost loved ones should never be silenced.
A reggae musician from Bagamoyo

Every stage name has a story, and Jhikoman’s is no different: JHIKO (from his first name, Jhikolabwino) plus MAN (from his surname, Manyika). Jhikoman has performed since 1994, blending acoustic reggae with African music and singing in English, Swahili, and his mother tongue, Kinyasa.

His musical life started at home. His older brother played guitar, and young Jhikoman watched, listened and dreamed. In secondary school, he fell for reggae, drawn by its messages of peace, love, unity, equality, and justice. He idolized Bob Marley and Alpha Blondy, and he covered their songs. Then his brother gave him the advice that changed everything: If you want to be a musician, write your own songs.
Jhikolabwino Siza Manyika performing at the Zanzibar International Film Festival. Photo by Micky Grapher, used with permission.

He took the advice to heart. In 1994, he stepped into a recording studio for the first time. In 2000, he released the album “Afro-Caribbean Beat,” and its title track became a local hit. The opportunities followed quickly. In 2001, he performed at the Zanzibar International Film Festival. In 2003, he wrote a song for Participatory Ecological Land Use Management (PELUM) Tanzania, an organization that supports small-scale farmers, and the commission took him to South Africa to perform at the World Forum for Sustainable Development. Since then, his music has carried him across East and Southern Africa and to stages in Europe.
Today he lives in Bagamoyo, where he volunteers as a music instructor at the Bagamoyo Institute of Arts and Culture and mentors young artists. He says:
“For me, music is more than entertainment. It is a powerful tool for communication, education, unity, and social change.”
The violence reaches home
The violence after the 2025 general election touched Jhikoman’s own circle. He says police shot and killed the wife of a close friend while she drove home, in front of her two children. He noted:

“No innocent person should lose their life simply because of violence surrounding an election. The victims and their families deserve justice, dignity, and the freedom to mourn without fear or intimidation.”

According to Jhikoman, the people who spoke out and wanted democratic reform often got silenced. They called for changes to election laws and procedures that would guarantee free, fair, transparent, and credible elections. They also demanded equal opportunities for all political parties, independent electoral oversight, and the freedom to choose their leaders without intimidation.
Why it’s so hard to get justice

Article 18 of Tanzania’s 1977 Constitution guarantees freedom of expression. Jhikoman says that some victims and their families have tried to enforce that right in court. However, getting justice has proved “extremely difficult.”

He points to several cases. After the alleged abduction of opposition activist Mpaluka Nyagali, known as Mdude, in May 2025, his wife filed a habeas corpus petition at the High Court in Mbeya. The court dismissed it on July 9, 2025, and his whereabouts remained unknown. A lawyer for former ambassador Humphrey Polepole filed a similar application after he disappeared in October 2025, and the court dismissed that as well.

Two advocates, Tito Magoti and Bob Wangwe, filed a case at the East African Court of Justice challenging the conduct of the election, and it remains pending. Authorities also arrested Tundu Lissu, chairman of the opposition party CHADEMA, and charged him with treason after he demanded electoral reforms. On November 6, 2026, the High Court acquitted him of treason, convicted him of incitement, and sentenced him to four years in prison. He remains imprisoned.
Jhikoman says:

“The law guarantees freedom of expression, but people who criticize the government face arrest, intimidation, and, in some cases, alleged abduction. The central problem is not simply the absence of laws; it is the difficulty of holding those responsible for violations accountable.”
A song that carries a message abroad

Listeners have responded well to Jhikoman’s message. He says that many Tanzanians feel the song finally carries their message to the international community. They believe the judiciary and parliament have lost their independence, which leaves them with little confidence that local institutions will deliver justice. Many now place their hope in international attention, because Tanzania has signed numerous international human rights agreements.
Some listeners also worry about his safety. They urge him to take care, since abductions and enforced disappearances remain serious concerns in parts of East Africa.

“I take those warnings seriously,” he says. “But I also believe that music can be a powerful tool for speaking out, raising awareness, and standing up for peace, justice, and the dignity of human life. … True peace means treating one another equally, standing up against injustice, respecting human rights, and giving everyone the freedom to express themselves without fear.”

Jhikoman’s story shows how justice shapes daily life long before anyone reaches a courtroom. When people trust that the justice system will treat them fairly and quickly, they speak out, report wrongdoings, and rebuild after loss. When they lose that trust, silence spreads. One reggae song cannot repair broken institutions, but it can name the problem, keep the memory of the dead in public view, and ask listeners to hold their leaders accountable.
Written by Zita Zage
542a6ebbdc134cae: The end of the working week is often enough to drive tech support people to drink, which is why The Register likes to get the party started early. Friday mornings bring a new installment of On Call – the column in which we share your stories of doing whatever it takes to keep tech running.
This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Bruce," who told us that in the mid-2000s he worked for a global radio station.
"We used to have about 30 PCs, all running slightly different radio shows depending on the time zone where we broadcast," he explained.
The PCs were old clunkers running Windows 95 long after Microsoft ended support for the OS. Management knew the machines needed replacing, but funding was probably another year away.
"We had to coax them on till then," Bruce wrote. "And by coax, I mean we were buying RAM on eBay because nobody sold the 4MB sticks we needed anymore."
Thanks to the tender ministrations of Bruce and his colleagues, the PCs kept humming and the radio stations stayed on the air.
Until a lovely spring Tuesday, when Bruce and his crew enjoyed a bucolic cup of tea in the first real sunshine of the season and received a call informing them that one of the stations was down.
One of Bruce's mates figured a cranky old PC probably just needed a reboot and headed off to fix it while the rest of the team enjoyed their tea.
And then the phone rang again to report another outage, so Bruce and the entire crew went back to work, chatting about which switch or other shared device could have taken out two PCs.
When they arrived in the office, the chap who had gone to reboot the first PC ran in and announced that the computer room had flooded.
Bruce and his teammates ran into that room and found dirty brown water all over the floor, walls, ceiling, and the racks holding the ancient PCs.
"Water was even spraying out of the front fans of the last two PCs that were still working," Bruce told The Register.

"After a lot of shouting words unfit to print, we all got to work ripping them out, shutting down what we could that looked to be working, and started lining them up outside in the car park," Bruce wrote. "Some of us then got to work stripping them down into component parts, others washed them down with isopropanol."
As the isopropanol supply dwindled, one of the team arranged an urgent delivery of vodka.
"Luckily, it was a gloriously sunny day, so we quickly rinsed the PCs and left them to dry, strewn all over the car park," Bruce wrote.
By this stage, he and the team were all filthy and exhausted. With the stations still offline, they had to rebuild the PCs and get them running again.
"We only lost two sticks of RAM, one sound card, and a power supply," Bruce wrote.
The culprit turned out to be a new hire on the facilities team who, while touring the building, had turned a random tap to see what would happen.

"It released water from a stagnant iron tank that sat there rusting away for years," Bruce wrote. For reasons nobody understood, the tank drained through a pipe into the room housing the broadcast PCs.

Have you had to clean up hardware in a hurry, perhaps with odd substances or implements? If so, click here to send On Call your story. We'll raise a glass to each one of you who sends a story and do it again if we share it on a future Friday. ®

1343a3d87eb0ded5: AWS now offers two new types of cloudy computers: emulated Androids and simulated iPhones.

The cloudy colossus announced both virtual offerings on Wednesday. They’re part of its Device Farm service, which previously saw AWS offer developers the chance to test their software on actual iOS and Android devices that reside in the Amazonian cloud. AWS will now also host virtual devices running Android and iOS.
AWS touts the virtual mobile devices as superior to physical devices.

“With virtual devices, you can shift testing left to stages that need high speed and volume, such as pull requests, code merges, and smoke tests, and keep real devices for later stages that need high fidelity, such as regression and release testing,” the cloudy business unit argues in its launch announcement.

AWS also says developers can get to work faster on a virtual iPhone or Pixel. “Virtual devices running the latest device and OS typically start in seconds, and others start in around a minute,” the outfit argues.
That may sound appetizing, but Amazon’s menu of virtual devices is short and bland.

When The Register logged on as an AWS user, the only emulated Android phone listed was a Google Pixel 10, running Android 15, 16, or 17. An emulated Pixel tablet running Android 17 is also on the menu.
At the time of writing, we could find only a virtual iPhone 16, running iOS 18.6, 23.61, and 27.0.
Analyst firm Counterpoint’s list of the world’s top 10 best-selling smartphones in Q2 of 2026 does not include a single Pixel device. The iPhone 16 occupies 10th place.
iPhone 17 models occupy the first, second, third, and seventh place on the list.

AWS might excite more developers if it adds emulators for the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, Galaxy A07 4G, A17 5G, A17 4G, and Galaxy S26, as they occupy the fourth, fifth, sixth, eighth and ninth places on Counterpoint’s list.
Amazon’s choice of a Pixel tablet is also an oddity given analyst firm IDC doesn’t list Google among its top five tablet vendors.

Amazon does offer physical Galaxy A17 devices and three versions of the iPhone 17. But Device Farm doesn’t offer any foldable devices, meaning developers struggling to wrap their heads around the iPhone Duo will need either ask Apple for a loaner or shell out $2,000 to acquire one.
At least developers don’t have to change behavior to access the few virtual devices AWS offers, as existing Device Farm APIs and test frameworks will work on real or notional machines. ®
