eefc75c7c3c24ae0: Years of technical debt, increasingly complex systems, and underinvestment in IT operations have left organizations vulnerable to major outages, according to Forrester.
The analyst pointed to a seven-day stretch in November when failures disrupted Microsoft 365, US air traffic control, banking, and other critical services.
The coinciding outages provoked "a slew of conspiracy theories about cyberattacks and AI," Forrester said.

"The real culprit is tragically mundane: the culmination of decades of technical debt, the frenetic buildout of massively complex and highly interdependent systems, the concentration of risk, and the underinvestment in advanced operations."

Forrester urged technology suppliers and in-house IT teams to prioritize resilience as their systems grow more complex. Otherwise, "the tech estate will collapse like a house of cards, taking down consumer and business trust with it."

Earlier this month, Microsoft was left struggling to restore many of its cloud services after a core process running on some servers became "overwhelmed" and its attempts to fix the problem failed. Some of its services did not recover for another 24 hours.

In October, Google Cloud blamed a "power event" for taking down multiple online products for customers in Western Europe. Affected services included BigQuery Data Transfer Service, Cloud Filestore, Cloud Run, Google App Engine, and Google Kubernetes Engine.
In October last year, a major outage impacted Amazon Web Services (AWS), with even Amazon's own web page reported to be offline and dozens of other online services and websites affected.

Aviation and banking were also hit this month. A communications outage triggered a nationwide ground stop in the US on November 13, while incidents involving JPMorgan Chase, United Airlines, Apple, Workday, Gmail, and other services added to the sense of widespread instability.
"Claims that these were all part of one connected cyberattack or conspiracy are highly unlikely. The real story is much more mundane," the report said.
Forrester argued that organizations have prioritized visible improvements over repairs to the underlying technology.

"Modernization investments have favored visible change over structural renewal," wrote report authors Lauren Nelson and Mark Moccia. "Organizations routinely fund new customer experiences, cloud migrations, platform consolidation, and AI initiatives because leaders can connect them to growth or productivity.

"They are less enthusiastic about updating core systems, simplifying architectures, retiring obsolete components, and eliminating fragile interfaces. The result is a modern front end resting on an aging, brittle, and increasingly interconnected estate."

Forrester's recommendations are to map dependencies, test failures and recovery under realistic conditions, and use incidents and near misses to identify weaknesses before they cause another outage. ®
8030417e575dab36: Britain's privacy watchdog is getting a taste of its own medicine, with an independent review set to examine the culture, governance, and accountability surrounding the events that led to former Information Commissioner John Edwards' resignation.
Karon Monaghan KC will examine whether the regulator's culture and governance allowed problems to develop or made concerns harder to raise.

Edwards quit in June after an independent workplace investigation found there was a "case to answer" over his behavior and that his conduct fell short of what was expected of a public official. He disagreed with some of its findings, but ultimately conceded that he had shown "poor judgment."

That investigation, however, focused on Edwards alone. According to the terms of reference published on Thursday, it "did not consider the wider conditions in which that conduct occurred, and it was not designed to."
The new review will cast a wider net. Monaghan wants to know whether staff could call out bad behavior further up the food chain, and what awaited those who tried.

It will also poke around the regulator's leadership and governance arrangements and its relationship with its sponsoring government department, including whether there were adequate ways for concerns to be escalated and those at the top to be challenged.

Current and former staff can give evidence confidentially and voluntarily, while Monaghan will be given access to relevant documents and existing material, including staff surveys and data on bullying, harassment and discrimination.
The ICO has confirmed it won't use confidentiality clauses in settlement agreements to prevent people from contributing to the review.

Monaghan decides which witnesses and documents are relevant, rather than the ICO or DCMS. Access remains subject to legal restrictions, and she must be told when material is withheld and why. She can speak to whoever she thinks is relevant and ask for the complaints, correspondence, and other paperwork she needs.

And if that leads her somewhere unexpected, she can ask to widen the investigation. DCMS can refuse, but it won't be able to quietly brush the request aside, and any decision not to expand the scope has to make it into the final report.
The review won't reopen the investigation into Edwards, make findings about the conduct of named individuals, or delve into the merits of the regulator's enforcement decisions.

Its arrival comes amid a broader shake-up at Britain's data watchdog. The old Information Commissioner's Office was formally replaced by the Information Commission on September 30, bringing with it a new board-led governance model.
The government first promised the wider review in July, shortly after Edwards' departure, but it didn't appoint its reviewer or nail down the terms until late November.
"We need to understand what is working, where things are falling short and, crucially, what needs to change," said DCMS Secretary Lisa Nandy.
The watchdog won't have to wait long for its report card. Monaghan is expected to deliver her findings in the first quarter of 2027, after which they will be published and handed to Parliament. ®
1ec52ab2acfcb198: Travel giant Flight Centre Travel Group (FLT) says "a significant number of customer records" may have been accessed by "unknown persons" following a cyberattack.
The Brisbane-headquartered company said the incident affected a third-party accommodation booking system used by Flight Centre, Travel Associates, Cruiseabout, and some independent travel agents.
Its disclosure [PDF], filed with the Australian Securities Exchange today, added that it was aware that records were accessed, but cannot definitively say how many were exfiltrated.
Flight Centre is working with the supplier and incident response specialist Mandiant to establish the scope of the incident.

An initial review suggests most accessed records contained only customer names, some with basic travel information. A "very small percentage" may also include birth dates, email addresses, limited passport details, phone numbers, or, in rare cases, health or mobility information.
Flight bookings and corporate travel use separate systems and are unaffected, the company said.

"FLT values customer privacy and data security," the company said in its disclosure. "The company understands that an incident like this can be unsettling for customers who may be affected, and we apologize for any concern this causes."
Investigations remain ongoing, but FLT has already contained the attack, rotated keys and credentials, and increased system monitoring, it said.
The company said it would contact affected customers directly. Its brands continue to operate normally, and travelers should proceed with their plans.
Customers should independently verify unexpected messages about their bookings before clicking links, opening attachments, or sharing personal information.
The attack on FLT follows others that have hit booking systems in the past year, including those on Booking.com and BWH Hotels.
More recently, another Australian business, RMS Cloud, which provides booking software to travel and leisure companies, also acknowledged a breach that led to WhatsApp scams in late October.
Numerous reports of travelers being targeted with messages that contained their names and booking details hit local news outlets at the time.
Customers were sent convincing messages seemingly from the hotels they had booked, and according to Australia's National Anti-Scam Centre, the scams appeared to be financially motivated.

Muhammad Yahya Patel, vCISO and cybersecurity advisor for EMEA at Huntress, said attackers targeting booking systems is a "familiar supply chain story" that has a greater impact than simple data theft.

Speaking generally about the risks of exposed travel records, Patel said: "Unlike a compromised email address or phone number, a passport can't be changed easily or quickly. For affected customers, the practical risk extends well beyond the immediate breach.

"Passport details combined with names, addresses, and travel history create a comprehensive identity profile that enables document fraud, identity theft, and targeted social engineering that could persist for years." ®
394e9f5b4e5d096c: Rackspace is shutting down its low-cost Spot cloud service after a security breach, giving customers two weeks' notice to move their workloads and retrieve their data.

In a notice posted on Tuesday, the cloud computing biz said its Rackspace Spot service will cease operations at 1700 Central Time (2300 UTC) on December 8. Any workloads still running at that point will be terminated, and customers will no longer be able to access their data.

"Following the recent security incident affecting Rackspace Spot, Rackspace has made the decision to wind down the service," the company said. "Spot customers are being notified with the wind-down timeline, instructions for retrieving their data and steps to secure their environments."
Customers will have to contend with the fallout from the breach while simultaneously trying to get their applications and data off the platform.

According to a customer notification seen by The Register, the attackers used leaked credentials to access parts of Rackspace Spot over a period of almost 22 hours on November 17. Rackspace only learned of the intrusion the following day, after a customer raised the alarm.
The intruders impersonated legitimate users, created pods in customer Kubernetes clusters, gained access to stored credentials known as Kubernetes Secrets, and listed nodes and storage volumes.
"With that access, they could have read any Secret in an affected user's clusters, and any Spot API token or refresh token that user held," Rackspace told customers.

Rackspace has since revoked the affected tokens and sessions, removed the pods planted by the intruders, and changed the affected platform and storage keys. Customers must also reissue API tokens, download new Kubernetes configuration files, and rotate credentials stored in their clusters, including database passwords and third-party API keys.
Sirish Raghuram, co-founder and chief growth officer of Platform9, which co-developed Spot with Rackspace, shed some light on the root cause in a November 20 GitHub post.
"An observability system was breached using a compromised credential," Raghuram wrote. "This was obviously a critical error on our part and we are very sorry we let this happen."
Raghuram said the incident necessitated significant changes to the underlying infrastructure clusters, prolonging the outage.

Spot's selling point was cheap compute. The service operated an auction-based pricing model, allowing customers to bid for cloud infrastructure at a fraction of the cost of conventional on-demand instances. Rackspace advertised savings of up to 90 percent for customers willing to tolerate interruptions to their workloads. A permanent interruption probably wasn't what they had in mind.

Rackspace hasn't explained why it chose closure over recovery, revealed how many customers were affected, or said whether it will offer migration extensions. It did not respond to The Register's questions. ®

c4a8d919d59815b3: Peninsula Energy has temporarily shut down its Wyoming uranium operation after a "cybersecurity incident" affected plant and wellfield control systems.

The Australian uranium producer said on Wednesday that it had activated its response procedures and brought in outside specialists following the attack on its US subsidiary, Strata Energy, which operates the Lance uranium project.

Peninsula Energy said it believes the attack is "confined to the plant and wellfield operating and control systems," and that back-office functions, such as payroll and other corporate systems, in both the US and Australia, remain unaffected.

"The company's immediate priorities have been to protect the safety of its employees, secure its operating systems, and work towards the restoration of operations in a safe and controlled manner," it said in an update to the Australian Securities Exchange.
The notification [PDF] went on to say that Peninsula Energy's investigations into the attack, including whether any data was compromised, remain ongoing.

Peninsula has not given a restart date and says it cannot yet assess the impact on its 2027 production guidance. Operations will remain suspended until recovery and safety checks are complete. "Peninsula will provide further updates to the market as material information becomes available," it said.
The disclosure of additional information came two days after Peninsula secured a short trading halt, which referenced a cybersecurity incident at its Wyoming site.
The November 23 filing [PDF] dated the incident to Friday evening in Western Australia. Wednesday's update clarified that Strata detected it on the morning of November 20, local US time.
Peninsula subsequently requested a voluntary suspension of trading until the earlier of November 30 or an announcement on restarting operations and any resulting change to production guidance.
Peninsula's Lance project is a uranium mining operation, extracting the element from underground deposits and turning it into uranium concentrate, aka yellowcake or U₃O₈.
Uranium concentrate is feedstock for nuclear fuel production, typically undergoing conversion, enrichment, and fabrication into uranium dioxide pellets before use in reactors.
The Lance central processing plant was constructed to produce a maximum of 2.0 million pounds (Mlb) of U₃O₈ annually, and is licensed for 3.0 Mlb.

Peninsula previously forecast production of 500,000 to 600,000 pounds in 2027, having withdrawn its 2026 guidance earlier this year following operational problems at Lance. It now says it will reassess the 2027 outlook once operations resume. ®
ec9fbbb151b965da: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we’re thankful every time someone leaves a password sticky note on a monitor or fails to delete a terminated employee’s admin account. But neither of those common occurrences is what we’ll be talking about today. Instead, our subject broke the number-one rule of backups: you gotta keep ’em separated.

Our story comes courtesy of Da Li, who serves as global alliance manager at Info2Soft, a company that provides data protection and recovery software. At one point, a partner called him into a case where a Chinese vehicle parts manufacturer fell victim to a ransomware gang. Unfortunately, its backup was compromised too.

The manufacturer had religiously backed up its manufacturing execution system (MES) and SAP orders, inventory, and finance systems every night. There was even a green dashboard that showed the backup process had succeeded, and someone checked that every morning.

However, one Friday evening, crims broke into the network and found out that the backup server was joined to the same Windows domain as the rest of the network. The hackers found a plaintext password for the backup service account in a maintenance script on a file share and discovered that someone had used the very same password for a domain admin account.
So the first thing the crooks did was delete every restore point on that backup server. Then they started encrypting the production servers to ransom them.
“Every backup job had succeeded for three years,” Li said. “The failure was that the thing meant to save them could be reached with the same keys as the thing being attacked.”
The results were devastating. With the MES and SAP data both gone, the plant couldn't schedule production, ship parts, or track them.

By the time Li was called in, the plant had already resolved its ransomware situation. We don’t know whether it paid or not. The manufacturer did ask Li and his company to make sure that this couldn’t happen again.

Li’s fix was not radical, but it was instructive. He made sure that the company now keeps its backup system outside the production domain, uses unique credentials, and requires MFA to reduce the risk of unauthorized access even if a password is compromised. He also made sure that the company keeps at least one offline backup and runs a test restore quarterly to ensure it’s prepared for emergencies.®

c9d929f7e8b12eb6: Much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems. But land use change is also a large component of the story, accounting for about one-third of total historical CO2 emissions. Deforestation plays a major role here, but practices like draining wetlands also factor in. Exactly how much of our history of eliminating wetlands has contributed to warming is challenging to figure out. But thanks to new sources of data that measure emissions from today’s surviving wetlands, it’s possible to put a better number on it.

A new study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—environments like bogs and fens where organic matter accumulates into thick layers of material. Some 600 billion tons of carbon are held in these vast stores of peat, which is more than you can find in all the world’s living vegetation, the researchers note.

Because these areas are permanently inundated, any oxygen in the water is quickly used up, leaving the job of decaying all that organic matter to anaerobic bacteria that work much more slowly and don't digest everything. So instead of seeing organic carbon turning into the CO2 gas released by aerobic bacteria, in peatlands, a subset of it gradually turns into methane gas. Methane is an even more potent greenhouse gas than CO2 itself and ultimately gets oxidized into CO2. That means there’s a little trade-off from peatlands—most of the carbon they have is kept out of the atmosphere, but the carbon that does escape does so as methane.

db125f4552756b9b: <!--kg-card-end: html--> Grand Theft Auto VI is 2026’s breakout entertainment event. By the numbers, it made roughly $3.79 billion in revenue at launch, outpacing the lifetime earnings for megahit films like Avatar, The Odyssey, and Avengers: Infinity War. PlayStation called it their biggest launch of all time with over 39 million players on the platform alone. It’s the center of the current cultural zeitgeist, whether it’s because of the game’s controversy, music, love story, cultural legacy, or its accolades.

Entire households are playing GTA VI with one slight hitch: unlike movies, TV shows, or even books you can read side by side, a single-player, 40+ hour experience is tough to enjoy when you live together.

For some couples, the solution has been using more than one console or even multiple copies of the game. Married couple Meagan Kelley and Kyle Prahl typically switch between playing different games in the same room, or the same platforms in different parts of the house. The two are parents who find time to game after putting their son to bed. “The nice thing about having really young kids is they do go to bed super early,” Kelley told me. “Usually [my son] goes down and is asleep before eight, so then that's kind of like our prime gaming time.” The couple often plays different games in the same room, but for GTA VI “we're playing separately, so that kind of sucks because it's like we don't get a lot of time for each other,” Kelley said.

Although some men online have whined about Grand Theft Auto VI’s central romance, complaining about doing favors for their in-game girlfriend Lucia (“cuck simulator” being one common refrain), Kelley says the benefits to her real-life relationship are only positive. “It's funny that there's so much online discourse about GTA splitting up relationships and stuff when it's like something that can bring Kyle and I closer,” Kelley said. “Especially as we become parents and need to have more perspective on making sure that we're making time for ourselves.”

Dividing up time to play and sharing their experiences, she said, adds a new dimension to their mutual hobby. “When we are together taking care of our kid or having conversations, it's almost like book club,” Kelley said. “We share the different ways that we're experiencing the game with choices and stuff like that.”

Justin Massongill, another GTA VI player, and his wife recently had their second child. “She's taken on a lot,” he said. He bought the game for her, giving her priority to play so she could de-stress.

Massongill watched his wife play the first hour of the game; the next morning, he started his own. “We're kind of trying not to look too much at the other player's screen,” he said. “I don't want to, you know, get spoiled on things. But it's also such a massive game that what are the chances that we're going to see the same thing in the first place?”

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> Madeline Blondeau and her fiancée decided to buy their copy of Grand Theft Auto VI together. The $80 price tag wasn’t so bad between the two of them; they downloaded the game, knowing that even with a PlayStation 5 and a PlayStation 5 Pro, they’d have to divvy up time between their single copy.

“We have been alternating our schedules,” Blondeau said. Her fiancée wakes up at 5 a.m. to start her IT job. Blondeau’s shift starts around 10 a.m. “We've sort of worked this out—me playing while she is working, and then her playing while I am finishing up my shift, trying to tiptoe around spoilers.”

Even as a queer couple, there’s an equality and care for each other in the experience Blondeau finds reassuring. “I think there's these very gendered expectations in relationships in terms of who games, who is the gamer of the household,” Blondeau said. You even see it in Grand Theft Auto, she adds, where Jason, the game’s male protagonist, will be the one with a controller in his hand. “Breaking down the gendered expectations of who is the gamer in the relationship really opens up a whole avenue for not getting into fights with your partner over video games,” Blondeau said.
“It feels like two people who figure their shit out, working out equitable time to experience something they've liked their whole lives, and talk about it.”

This past weekend, Blondeau’s fiancé left to grab groceries. She came back with something extra: the Grand Theft Auto trilogy for Nintendo Switch, a consolation prize for whoever wasn’t playing their shared copy of GTA VI. “I was in the mood to play Vice City,” her partner said. “We can trade off."

In Scotland, the Scottish National Party (SNP) posted GTA 6 memes so cringe that they talked about it on the floor of parliament. On November 19, the SNP social media accounts posted AI-generated pictures of Boris Johnson and Margaret Thatcher in the GTA style. “When the loading screen so long you start seeing characters you’ve never seen before,” one image said over a picture of Thatcher pouring a bag of “Scottish oil money” into the UK treasury.

Scotland’s Green Party didn’t find the memes funny. Rockstar is originally Scottish, was founded in Edinburgh, and still maintains a significant studio there. In parliament, Green co-leader Gillian Mackay said she was proud of what all of Rockstar’s workers had done to stand up against bad working conditions and produce a work of art like GTA 6. Then she made comments about SNP leader and Scottish First Minister John Swiney.

“Last night the SNP angered anti-AI campaigners by posting AI-generated GTA memes on its social media despite huge concerns about the impact of AI and AI data centers on artists, workers, and the environment,” Mackay said in the parliament session. “Does the first minister understand why people are concerned about his government’s approach to AI and the big companies behind it.”

The SNP deleted the memes and Swiney apologized. “First of all, let me say that I don’t want to offend anyone by anything that we get up to, so if I’ve offended anyone about that, I’m sorry about that. It was not my intention,” Swiney said in the Scottish parliament. Then he said he shared concerns about AI but defended the technology’s use for healthcare.

There will be more bad posts like this. Grand Theft Auto VI hasn’t been out for even a week and the memetic landscape around it will shift and change. We don’t even know what the dominant memes for the game are yet, let alone the innovative ways posters will iterate on them. Rest assured, however, that the governments of the world are watching and waiting to post their own variations and make it all cringe.

3e44a71fc7f63f38: More than eight years after Rodrigo Duterte announced the Philippines would withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC), the country’s former president is about to begin his trial in The Hague. Duterte faces charges of crimes against humanity over alleged killings carried out during his deadly war on drugs. The trial, which begins on 30 November, comes at a precarious moment for the court, as the United States ramps up its efforts to undermine the institution. “Nothing has really quite approached this level of hostility we’re seeing coming from President Trump, or more particularly Marco Rubio,” explains Carrie McDougall, an associate professor at Melbourne Law School, speaking on The Conversation Weekly podcast. The US has never joined the ICC, citing concerns about politically motivated prosecutions of its nationals. But the court can investigate alleged war crimes committed by Americans on the territory of its member countries. McDougall says the US has “made no bones” about its opposition to the investigation of US nationals and the prosecution of Israeli nationals. In October, the Trump administration extended sanctions against individual ICC judges and prosecutors to the court as a whole. The sanctions threaten the court’s access to banking and IT services, as well as its ability to engage with victims and witnesses, McDougall says. The US has also been pressuring countries to withdraw from the court. McDougall attributes the decisions by Venezuela, Chad and Nauru to withdraw from the ICC to that pressure. Meanwhile, Duterte’s case illustrates both the powers and limitations of the court. “The reality is that the court itself doesn’t have any enforcement powers,” McDougall says. Instead, it relies on the Security Council – which has never used its enforcement powers to assist the court – and countries to cooperate with it. Duterte was arrested by his own country’s authorities. Russian President Vladimir Putin and Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu are both subject to ICC arrest warrants, but Russia and Israel have refused to cooperate in the arrest of their leaders. Neither country is a member of the ICC. While the ICC doesn’t have its own enforcement powers, arrest warrants still have some power; they can restrict leaders’ ability to travel overseas and potentially deter others from committing crimes. And, McDougall says: There is no statute of limitations, so those ICC arrest warrants can be enforced after individuals have lost power and lost the protection of their states. Duterte’s case also demonstrates that withdrawing from the ICC does not necessarily shield political leaders from prosecution, explains McDougall. Once a state … files a notice of withdrawal, it takes a year to become effective, and the ICC retains jurisdiction over any crimes committed up until that effective withdrawal date. So will the ICC survive? McDougall says the US sanctions “will impede the court’s ability to fulfil its mandate” and that the threat is “very serious.” She also warns that US attacks on international institutions risk emboldening other countries, including China and Russia, that want to reshape that order. “I think we are facing something of a crossroads,” she says. McDougall describes the ICC as the “canary in the coal mine” for the international legal order: It is required to hold to account those responsible for international crimes, particularly when we’re talking about the leaders of states. And so that puts a really big target on its back for would-be spoilers. Ultimately, though, McDougall does not expect a mass exodus from the ICC. I think a lot will actually hinge on how robustly other ICC states’ parties stand up for the court. 38bebe8b01f35c10: TOKYO, Nov 26 — US President Donald Trump’s fresh tariff blitz aims to pressure Asian countries into sealing trade deals with Washington so as to avoid unfavourable duty rates, analysts said on Thursday.
The proposed levies announced on Wednesday affect a range of nations in the region, from long-time US competitor China to allies like South Korea and Japan.
They could result in rates of up to 20 per cent on exports from the targeted countries, but face a period of public comment before taking effect, at the earliest in January.

The announcement came after Washington concluded a months-long probe into alleged excess production in the targeted economies, which itself followed the US Supreme Court’s decision ruling that Trump’s previous “Liberation Day” duties were illegal.
But “several of these economies already have prior negotiated tariff rates with the US, which would effectively cap the appliable rate”, said MUFG economist Lloyd Chan in a note.
The US has also indicated that the new tolls will not stack on top of other tariffs already imposed on 60 countries over forced labour concerns. Instead, the higher rate will apply.
“In all, that should help contain the incremental tariff shock, assuming prior negotiated commitment remains in place,” Chan said.
However, it does mean that Washington has established higher tariff ceilings that can be activated “should trade negotiations or existing commitments break down”, he added.
Stephen Brown of Capital Economics also noted that “the US has left open its ability to hike these tariffs if trade agreements fall apart”, particularly with China.
Room for leverage
In Beijing’s case, the new levies stand at 20 per cent, meaning the total rate could jump to 40 per cent if its current trade truce with Washington, set to expire in January, is not extended.
Such a scenario “could take the two largest economies back to the trade wars of 2025”, Josh Lipsky, of the Atlantic Council, wrote in a note.
However, that is not something Trump wants, he added.
Instead, the US president is banking on an extension of the truce, though this is “far from a sure thing”, Lipsky added.
Trump and China’s Xi Jinping are set to meet next in December at the G20 summit in Miami.
“Tariff wars and trade wars are not in anyone’s interest,” Beijing’s foreign ministry warned on Wednesday.
Other Asian economies, also in Trump’s crosshairs due to significant trade imbalances, are likewise under pressure.
Vietnam faces a maximum additional tariff of 35 per cent on goods, which could be cut to 20 per cent if a trade deal is reached.
Hanoi reiterated on Wednesday that it has made commitments under a framework agreement in October 2025, and that it is working for a final deal “as soon as possible”.
India uncertain, Taiwan bullish
India said on Wednesday that trade concerns should be addressed in ongoing talks with Washington for a bilateral trade deal.
The US has proposed a 17 per cent rate on Indian goods, rising to a possible 25 per cent if no deal is reached.
The countries reached an interim agreement in February aimed at reducing US tariffs on Indian goods.
But the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s levies days later, fuelling uncertainty over when the agreement would take effect.

“By deploying a dual-rate structure — threatening steep baseline tariffs against countries that refuse a pact while offering lower rates to those that sign — Washington reclaims the bargaining power to impose duties at will and extract unilateral concessions,” Ajay Srivastava, founder of the Global Trade Research Initiative, told Bloomberg News.
In contrast with Indian uncertainty, Taiwan, which reached a deal with Washington in early 2026, struck a reassuring tone.

“We are confident that when tariffs are finalised early next year, we will return to a 15 per cent non-stacked tariff under the agreement between Taiwan and the US,” Vice Premier Cheng Li-chiun told a news briefing. — AFP

c726a5af6b120d4c: Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he’s cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it’s wired up to nerves in the upper part of his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can use his left limb to handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, and a loved one’s hand.

Davidson, who is taking part in a clinical trial run by the University of Utah, is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted in his arm. But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently.

The hand is part of the bionic LUKE arm, named after Luke Skywalker of Star Wars, who was fitted with a lifelike prosthetic arm after his own was light-sabered off. The arm was developed in the 2000s, initially trialed in 2014, and approved by the FDA that same year. The trial that Davidson is enrolled in isn’t so focused on the arm itself but on a new way to connect it to a person’s nervous system. The connection allows users to control movements and receive feedback about how much pressure they’re applying.

Researchers hope that Davidson’s experiences will help them answer some long-standing questions about the technology, including how useful it really is in day-to-day life. They want to know when the device is helpful and where it might fail. They also want to learn how it might affect Davidson’s well-being as well as his brain and nervous system.
The loss of a limb

In 2009, when he was 16, Davidson climbed a telephone pole to get the best shot of a sunset. “I climbed about 35 feet up,” he recalls. But he lost his footing as he tried to descend. He grabbed for a wire, which ended up electrocuting him, before he fell to the ground.

The accident resulted in second- and third-degree burns over 37% of his body, says Davidson, “and I broke my back in approximately 50 separate locations.” He also broke eight ribs, and his spinal cord was severed. He’s pretty sure he broke his left wrist, too. But around 10 days later, his left hand—his dominant hand, and the one he’d grabbed the wire with—had started to develop gangrene. It was amputated.

Davidson was ultimately in a coma for around a month. “Once I woke up, they explained to me: You’re paralyzed, you’re never going to walk again, and also, we took your left hand,” he recalls. “A bit of an inconvenience at 16, to say the least.”

Davidson, now 33 and a trauma therapist, went on to have physical therapy and adjusted to life in his changed body. He’s tried a range of prosthetic hands. The first one, which he received a year and a half after his injury, was a basic hook that allowed him to pick things up. It wasn’t fancy, but it gave him “a psychological feeling of returning to being whole,” he says.

The hands he’s tried since have been more advanced—some have allowed him to control individual fingers with muscle movements, for example. Some have been covered by his medical insurance, which allows for replacements around every five years, he says. Others he’s had to buy himself. He bought his third prosthetic hand, for example, from eBay. “It’s funny to think I bought a secondhand second hand,” he says.
New connections

A chance encounter with a scientist at a supermarket introduced Davidson to the research team at the University of Utah, which specialized in researching devices that plug into the body. Since 2013, the team had been running a trial of a system that could connect with the nerves of a residual limb, allowing an amputee to control a bionic one. Davidson turned out to be an ideal candidate, says Jake George, director of the university’s neurorobotics lab.

Davidson, who was keen to take part, first had to undergo what George describes as “pretty extensive” physical and psychological evaluations. Not only did he have to be well enough for surgery, but the team also scanned his brain to make sure that he still had a mental representation of his left hand—suggesting he’d be able to move a bionic one. They also ran tests to check that the nerves in his arm were working.

A therapist evaluated Davidson’s motivations for taking part in the trial. “Our patients aren’t being compensated, they don’t get to keep the device, and they go through two surgeries—the surgery to get it in and the surgery to take it out,” says George. “Avi’s doing this because he wants to help others.”

In late January of this year, Davidson flew from Florida to Utah to undergo his first surgery. It was a fairly complicated procedure involving engineers as well as a full surgical team. “We [researchers] stand in the back of the room and basically answer the question when the surgeon asks, ‘Where do I put the damn thing?’” says George. The surgeon exposed three nerves in Davidson’s arm and implanted an electrode array containing 100 needles in each one.

Nerves are floppy, so pushing electrodes into them doesn’t do much, says George. Instead, the team connected the electrodes to the nerves using what he describes as a “compressed-air gun.” “You shoot the grid of needles into the nerve at a very, very high velocity,” he says.

The team also inserted 24 electrodes into the muscles around the nerves. Wires for each of the nerve arrays and for pairs of muscle electrodes were left protruding from Davidson’s skin. After the surgery, he was offered some time to recover. “By day two, I’m like ‘No, let’s get me on the machines,’” he says.
COURTESY OF AVI DAVIDSON
That next step involved training a computer system to essentially translate the electrical activity in Davidson’s nerves into signals for bionic hand and wrist movements.

To get it up and running, the team had to train the device in two directions. The first involved converting nerve activity into hand, wrist, and finger movements. The researchers did this by listening in on the signals collected from the hundreds of electrical connection points in Davidson’s arm while he thought about various movements. That part was easy, says George: “It takes a matter of about five minutes.”

The second direction—linking the electrodes to sensations felt by the prosthetic—is much more time-consuming. Team members would stimulate each of the electrode connection points in turn, asking Davidson if he felt anything. They’d then turn up the signal at each of those points to see the effect. “It’s like a three-day process,” says George.
Becoming bionic

Davidson’s wires have since been connected and simplified, says George, who describes the process as “more or less like plugging in an HDMI cord or a USB-C cord.” When he wants to use his prosthetic, Davidson must first put it on, connect it to the wires, and then initiate it using a small computer.

He’s also had to undergo extensive physical therapy to learn how to control the hand. After all, it’s nothing like the prostheses he’s used in the past. “It’s almost like learning a different language with this kind of technology,” says Leanne Seckinger, an occupational therapist at the University of Utah Health System, who works with Davidson.

At first, she and Davidson worked on learning to hold and stabilize objects. They focused on Davidson’s personal goals—he wanted to be able to cook at home, so the pair worked on strategies to hold and manipulate utensils, prepare and chop ingredients, and carry plates and bowls. “He was able to crack an egg,” says Seckinger. “He made an omelet.”

Davidson has been using the hand at home since July 10, and he has noticed improvements. At first it took him a few minutes to write his name; now he can manage it in seconds. “The things I’m able to do with it now are tremendous, comparatively to where I was at initially,” he says.
Today, he says, he wears the hand around six days a week. He changes the batteries once or twice during the day and takes it off overnight. It’s heavy, weighing in at around five pounds, he says.

The hand can be useful, but it has also proved surprising. Sometimes, Davidson feels pain in it. This could be what’s known as “phantom pain”—a symptom experienced by some people who have lost a limb.

Curiously, he also says he experiences wrist strain. Davidson says he’s been getting a stiffness in his prosthetic wrist similar to what he experiences when he’s been typing for a long time with his flesh-and-blood right hand. He’s also realized that he can relieve the tension by pulling the bionic fingers back to stretch out his prosthetic wrist. “It’s weird,” he says.

The phenomenon “makes no sense physiologically,” says Chris Duncan, a rehabilitation doctor and chief medical officer at BIOS, a neurotechnology company that is supporting the trial. Stretching a typical hand pulls on tendons that extend down the forearm. There aren’t any tendons in a bionic arm—Davidson’s “stretches” are just moving actuators, says Duncan. He doesn’t know why it’s helpful but suspects it might have something to do with how the hand is represented in his mind. “What Avi’s experiencing is kind of like uncharted territory, honestly,” he says.

The research team is currently planning a bigger study and hopes to get the two-way sensation device approved by the FDA so that it can be covered by health insurance. “They need to understand that this is a useful new technological paradigm that will bring value to patients,” says Duncan. Team members also hope the technology will allow users to operate other devices, such as remote controls and wheelchairs.

Davidson will have his implants and the hand for a couple more months at least. But the trial was designed to run for “at least” one year, and that year will be up by the end of January 2027. “I’m not quite sure what happens after that,” he says.
George hopes the trial could be extended, but that will depend on funding. “From our perspective, we’d like to go as long as we can,” he says. “We don’t want to leave Avi without support.”

Davidson isn’t too worried about what comes next, though. “I went into this knowing that this was not something that I get to keep,” he says. “I am not going to benefit from this … I wanted to be a part of this in the context of being able to help push the technology forward.”

f067e2f75ccbe3a4: Donate to our Independent Journalism Spotlight issue, and get more of the coverage you value!
Originally published on Global Voices
Image made via Canva Pro. All images fair use.

Journalism has been a vital part of society for centuries. Writing about what happened and sharing it with others; reading about what happened somewhere else and discussing it with those around you; having a platform for letters, comments, and opinion about everything from the niche to the rich. Journalism has toppled governments and CEOs, revealed complicated scams, brought out the beauty of ethnographically observed daily life, recorded our qualms and foibles for posterity, and whipped up outrage, empathy, and triumph.

But journalism is on a precipice. The shift from print to digital has opened up new possibilities, as well as vulnerabilities. Changes in how we interact, especially at a distance, have changed what (and how) people want to read, listen to, or watch to understand the news.

This decade has seen dramatic changes in the field, from the loss of foundational trust in the institution, to digital, legal, and physical threats to journalists to the near-complete erosion of financial security for people who carry out this work. Increasingly authoritarian governments turn on the media, and the press in countries from Hong Kong to Myanmar to Russia to Nicaragua has been forced into exile.

Even countries such as the UK and the US have seen government targeting of journalists for critical reporting. Israel’s genocide in Gaza has laid bare the hypocrisy of the international press establishment, causing a crisis of confidence, while small local news outlets and independent journalists continue to report despite this.

Through it all, journalists have kept documenting, analyzing, responding, and reporting, even when they are underpaid and overworked, face hostile governments and terrible technology, sometimes from exile, in terrible conditions, even at risk of their lives. As we begin 2027, Global Voices will turn the spotlight onto these voices that continue to speak truth to power and bring to light the news that we all need to know. We will look at civic journalism, find out what is changing, and meet some of these indefatigable defenders of our right to free speech and our right to information.

0cd88d2cf652a020: Mikhail Svetlov/Getty ImagesAs early as December. That’s how soon Russia could put a satellite carrying a nuclear weapon in orbit, according to German media reports. If the news sounds familiar from headlines past, that’s because it is. In 2024, the United States made a similar allegation, albeit without giving any potential launch window. These latest reports claim that the satellite, Sputnik-S, was assembled several years ago and is in storage near Moscow. Intelligence agencies in NATO countries have reportedly shared information about the satellite. This week, the alliance’s secretary general asserted that protecting NATO territory includes keeping it safe from threats to space systems. Russia’s embassy in Berlin said it “categorically reject[s] all these groundless allegations”. Echoing Moscow’s 2024 denial, it called the reports “propaganda”, adding that Russia “strictly adheres to the fundamental 1967 Outer Space Treaty”. What is this treaty and what does it say about nuclear weapons? And how could the international community respond or even verify what is on board a satellite? A lesson on cooperation The prospect of nuclear weapons off-Earth helped drive negotiations for the treaty invoked by Russia. During the Cold War, the US and the Soviet Union found common ground on keeping these weapons out of orbit. It was a lesson on cooperation, despite competition and conflict, worth recalling in what is framed as today’s “space race”. A cornerstone of international space law that prevails to this day, the Outer Space Treaty is also an arms control treaty. Under Article IV, countries undertake not to: place in orbit around the Earth any objects carrying nuclear weapons or any other kinds of weapons of mass destruction, install such weapons on celestial bodies, or station such weapons in outer space in any other manner. Placing a nuclear weapon in orbit would itself breach the prohibition, even if it was never detonated. If a detonation did occur, it would breach the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty of 1963, which prohibits nuclear explosions in outer space and in the atmosphere. Read more: Too many satellites? Earth’s orbit is on track for a catastrophe – but we can stop it A nuclear ‘aurora’ No country is known to have ever placed a nuclear weapon in orbit. But there are examples from history of states detonating nuclear weapons off-Earth. One summer’s night in 1962, people in Hawai'i gazed upward and saw what was, in effect, a nuclear “aurora”. One eyewitness, then a teenager, who was watching with her sibling from a spot overlooking Pearl Harbor, recalled the “exploding sky” and how it later turned “a deep blood red that lingered”. The US had detonated a nuclear weapon about 400 kilometres above the Pacific Ocean in a classified test code-named Starfish Prime. The US and the Soviet Union were testing nuclear weapons in space almost in lockstep, each demonstrating its advancing technological capabilities. Starfish Prime was more than a visual spectacle. Of the 24 satellites in orbit at the time or launched in the following weeks, at least a third suffered damage. The Starfish Prime ‘aurora’ seen from Honolulu. Capnez/Wikimedia What happens in space is a threat on Earth Today, the European Space Agency estimates there are about 15,800 functioning satellites in Earth’s orbit. These satellites support the critical infrastructure we rely on every day, from navigation for transport to timing for banking and telecommunications. Whether we realise it or not, we are all “space citizens”. Some satellites also support nuclear command, control and communications functions. Others give early warning of missile attacks. Researchers at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute examine this “space–nuclear nexus”. During a conflict, leaders might interpret an attack on an early-warning satellite as “a precursor to a nuclear-first strike”. How they respond to that ambiguity could have escalatory risks and significance. Mitigating the threat through verification So, what can the global community do to mitigate possible and actual threats of nuclear weapons in space? As a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council, Russia could veto a resolution responding to the current allegation. Indeed, in 2024, it vetoed a US–Japan draft resolution reaffirming the Article IV prohibition. The Outer Space Treaty sets out no specific procedure for verifying whether a satellite carries a nuclear weapon, nor does any other international instrument. Three think tanks working on global and space security have led expert dialogues on how to do so. In their latest joint report, they conclude that verification is “feasible”, albeit challenging, and should be pursued even if “progress may be incremental”. The report canvasses multiple options. These include nations working together to test ways of detecting a nuclear weapon in orbit, agreeing on how to handle disputed evidence, and inviting pre-launch inspections. In my research, I have been exploring how nuclear safeguards could advance non-proliferation by verifying nuclear material on board a space object before launch. As global nuclear arsenals continue to expand and modernise, we must not lose hope of a world one day free of nuclear weapons, an aspiration reflected in the disarmament pillar of the Non-Proliferation Treaty of 1968. The onus must also rest heavily on states actually capable of launching nuclear-armed satellites, whether or not they face allegations. The US, China and Russia could discuss verification options in the trilateral dialogue they recently agreed to hold on nuclear risk. In a strained geopolitical context, a nation’s verbal reassurances alone are unlikely to give the global community the confidence it needs. Nations agreed nearly 60 years ago to keep nuclear weapons out of space. Verifying whether they keep that commitment will take cooperation, too. Art Cotterell's postdoctoral fellowship is co-funded by the UNSW Nuclear Innovation Centre and UNSW Law & Justice. He is affiliated with the Australasian Centre for Space Governance.
a3894a1164fefbce: The Conversation, CC BY-SATo get the most out of Black Friday sales, a bit of research is always useful. Ideally, this involves working out what you might want to buy – and checking prices – before sales begin. Once the sales are under way, comparing prices, delivery costs and delivery times at different stores can feel onerous and time-consuming, especially if you’re worried you might miss out on a deal. To streamline their search for a bargain, some shoppers are turning to artificial intelligence (AI) tools to do the research for them. Can AI really help you snag a deal? The answer is yes, maybe. But there are reasons to proceed carefully. Sending bots on a bargain hunt AI is being used to take the legwork out of all sorts of tasks. It makes sense consumers across the world are increasingly putting it to work as a shopping companion. Say you’re looking for a new coffee machine or laptop this Black Friday. Rather than trawl through dozens of different sites yourself, you might ask a tool such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini to search the web for you and prepare a spreadsheet with a list of options. A recent survey by the Australian Retail Council and market research firm Roy Morgan found this Black Friday, one in four respondents were planning to use an AI chatbot for research. Among this group, 72% said it would be their first time doing so. If you fall into this category, there are a few things to be aware of as you check any recommendations. Bogus bargains, ‘ghost stores’ and ads Hallucination is a well-known feature of generative AI tools. In the context of shopping with AI, this means some products, prices and stores may be entirely made up or misinterpreted. A related concern is whether AI tools can reliably distinguish between genuine online stores and the fake or “ghost stores” that spring up online during sales periods. Then, of course, there’s advertising. Many AI tools, including the free and low-cost versions of OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google Search’s AI Overview and AI Mode, have already started rolling out advertising. Both OpenAI and Google say advertisements shown to users are clearly labelled. But depending on your settings, the ads you see may be informed by your previous conversations with these tools. Other generative AI tools don’t have ads. Anthropic, for example, has pledged to keep Claude ad-free. And Google’s Gemini app remains free of advertising, at least for now. The other side of the checkout Even if you decide not to use AI this Black Friday, it could still shape the deals you see. Some retailers are reportedly already using AI to guide their discounting strategies. AI is already changing the way companies decide what discounts to offer to everyone. Ashkan Forouzani/Unsplash This includes using sophisticated models and past sales data to work out the smallest discount they need to offer to sell a product. Another potential headwind for shoppers is the use of AI by retailers to personalise prices to the amount a consumer is likely to be prepared to pay, sometimes called “surveillance pricing”. Currently, this is not explicitly against the law unless the surveillance pricing involves discrimination based on protected characteristics such as race, sex or disability. Read more: AI is using your data to set personalised prices online. It could seriously backfire Handing over your wallet By Black Friday next year, new tools which go beyond simple research may be more commonplace: AI shopping agents. These tools can find stores selling what you’re looking for, compare prices and then complete the purchase on your behalf. For example, Meta’s Muse agent, which launched in Australia last week, integrates with existing social media accounts and can complete tasks on your behalf. Other tech companies are also venturing into the space. OpenAI recently launched its Dots agent, and Google’s offerings include Agentic Checkout and Gemini Tasks. Amazon offers its own shopping agent but blocks other third-party agents from accessing its site. Can we make agents safe? Developers such as Meta say they are building in protections to prevent consumer AI agents “going rogue” and overstepping their authority or spending instructions. But even with safeguards in place, other risks could be amplified. AI agents rely on “context” to execute the purchases their consumers are likely to prefer. Essentially, this means information about your previous interactions is used to predict what you might want in the future. More broadly, there is the risk AI tools may not be working in shoppers’ best interests. An OECD paper this month warned commercial partnerships could shape which products and prices AI tools recommend, in ways that may not be understood by shoppers. The federal government has flagged new laws may be needed to respond to the rise of AI shopping agents, including to guard against manipulation or exploitative personalised pricing. Some old-fashioned common sense So, what’s the advice? By all means, use AI to find a Black Friday bargain, if you choose. But be sceptical. Treat its recommendations as just one piece of information. It is worth checking the policies of your preferred AI tool to see if you can turn off its memory of earlier chats. You may also be able to limit advertising and prevent your prompts from being used for training. Ultimately, getting the best deal still means weighing up your options, sticking to a budget and thinking about whether you really need what’s on sale.
